newsitem.title: UK: Washington urged to halt UK-US open skies talks.
newsitem.headline: Washington urged to halt UK-US open skies talks.

text.p: Five U.S. airlines asked the new U.S. Transport Secretary on Tuesday to hold up long-running aviation trade talks with Britain for a public investigation into the British Airways, American Airlines tie-up.

United Airlines said its chief executive Gerry Greenwald and counterparts at four other carriers have written to Rodney Slater asking that a full public investigation be undertaken into the alliance to establish the terms for negotiating an open skies trade agreement with Britain.
The other carriers are Delta Air Lines, TWA, Tower Air, and privately owned transatlantic holiday airline Laker Airways.

"The Department of Transportation should immediately begin to conduct a through investigation of the proposal (for the alliance) as well as U.S.-UK market conditions prior to proceeding with bilateral negotiations," the airline said in a joint statement released here.
They said the key issue was access to London Heathrow and the need to settle differences over whether rivals could compete there against BA and American.

"These are major factual disputes affecting DOT's ability to evaluate the alliance properly and to formulate an appropriate aviation negotiating policy with the UK. If the critical underlying facts are misunerstood the Department's analysis will be fatally flawed," they said.

The request echoed a similar call made last year by several of the airlines in a letter sent to President Clinton urging him to halt the open skies talks with Britain until Washington had settled whether it could approve the BA and American alliance.
But the U.S. government's response that time was to say open skies talks would continue as planned.
The next round of talks between the two governments are due to be held in Washington on February 4.

Airline industry sources have said next week's round is not expected to reach agreement but will instead keep the negotiating process ticking over while Britain continues with its own investigation into the BA deal with American.

Britain has said approval of the alliance is the key to getting an open skies deal, since it would allow BA to compete for transatlantic transfer traffic in the huge U.S. domestic market where only U.S. airlines are allowed to operate.
Conversely the U.S. government has made an open skies deal which opens up landing rights into London Heathrow as a condition for allowing the deal to pass U.S. anti-trust laws.
Under the proposed alliance BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

BA and American argue that their deal will lead to greater competition because an open skies deal would allow all U.S. airlines access to compete at Heathrow, the most popular of Europe's transatlantic landfalls.

Under the current bilateral aviation treaty only four airlines are allowed to operate services out of Heathrow -- BA, Virgin Atlantic, United Airlines and American -- and frequencies and routes are restricted.
But BA and American's rivals including United and Virgin say BA and American should give up landing slot times at Heathrow to make room for more competition.

British trade minister Ian Lang proposed in December conditions for allowing the alliance through, with a core demand that BA release 168 weekly runway slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights -- to make room for competitors.

Critics of the deal have told Lang's Office of Fair Trading in a review of his proposals that more than the 168 slots need to be given up, at competitive times of the day, as well as ground facilities.
